principles.name: Be curious, learn fearlessly
principles.description: Part of 'Think Really Big': stay curious, keep learning new technology and domains, and grow capabilities over time without fear of looking inexperienced.
evidence_signals: Learned a new technology, protocol or domain quickly and applied it to real work
Shows how their capabilities grew over time, not a fixed skill set
Asks questions and seeks out unfamiliar problems instead of avoiding them

principles.name: Take smart risks and innovate
principles.description: Part of 'Think Really Big': take calculated risks, innovate, adapt when things change, and try again.
evidence_signals: Started an improvement on their own initiative and explains why the risk was worth it
Limited the downside of a risk with a pilot, rollback plan or staged rollout
Adapted the approach after a setback and tried again

principles.name: Be real, be coachable
principles.description: Part of 'Play to Win': be authentic, own mistakes honestly, and seek and act on coaching and feedback.
evidence_signals: Describes a mistake or failure honestly, without blaming others
Asked for feedback or coaching and shows what changed afterwards
Tells their own story in their own words rather than a polished script

principles.name: Speak up, debate, and commit
principles.description: Part of 'Play to Win': raise concerns openly, debate ideas with respect, then commit fully to the decision.
evidence_signals: Raised a disagreement early and stated the other view fairly
Used data or a test to settle a debate
Committed to and supported a decision that went against their own view

principles.name: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability
principles.description: Part of 'Play to Win': deliver high-quality work with a sense of urgency and own the result, including what goes wrong.
evidence_signals: Uses 'I' for own decisions and owns the outcome end to end
Delivered under time pressure without cutting quality on what matters
Kept or renegotiated commitments openly and followed through after launch

principles.name: Drive customer outcomes
principles.description: Part of 'Drive Durable Growth': focus on outcomes for customers, with products and experiences they value, and favor reliability and customer needs over internal convenience.
evidence_signals: Names a specific customer or user group and the result for them
Chose reliability or customer need over the easier engineering option
Measures success in customer terms such as uptime, adoption or resolved issues

principles.name: Embrace One Cisco
principles.description: Part of 'Drive Durable Growth': work as one company across teams, regions and products, build on the platform, connect work to company priorities and purpose, and include and bring others along.
evidence_signals: Collaborated across teams, time zones or business units to deliver a shared result
Helped a colleague or another team succeed and included different perspectives
Connects own work to broader company or platform goals

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Two or three coding problems plus multiple-choice questions on networking, operating systems and databases, as reported by prep sites. Common for early-career hiring; not every team uses it. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, interest in Cisco, role fit and logistics. Held over Webex or phone. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Resume discussion plus one live coding problem and CS or networking fundamentals. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding rounds
rounds.notes: One or two live coding rounds in the final loop, often with graph or tree problems. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Domain and fundamentals deep dive
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior software engineer from the hiring team
rounds.notes: Verbal questions in the team's domain: networking protocols (TCP/IP, OSI, routing), operating systems and concurrency, or cloud and security, plus a past-project deep dive. Domain varies by team.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Mainly for experienced candidates. Whiteboard design with a networking angle: monitoring for many devices, load balancers, control planes, Webex-like real-time systems. Not simulated in v1 as a whiteboard round; verbal design questions appear under technical_qa patterns.

rounds.name: Behavioral and values
rounds.notes: STAR-style questions on failure, conflict, customer focus and working across global teams, tied to Cisco's culture. Prep sites report behavioral topics carry heavy weight.

rounds.name: Hiring manager conversation
rounds.notes: Past projects, motivation, scope and team fit. Sometimes merged with the behavioral round; duration is a common-pattern estimate.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: PM background, B2B and enterprise experience, motivation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Product experience, approach to enterprise products, prioritization and stakeholder management.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: An enterprise or networking product problem: strategy, roadmap prioritization or a market opportunity. Some teams ask for a prepared presentation.

rounds.name: Technical and platform discussion
rounds.notes: APIs, platform dependencies and how scale, reliability and security constraints shape product choices.

rounds.name: Cross-functional interviews
rounds.notes: Several conversations on influence without authority, misalignment across teams and working with sales and channel partners.

rounds.name: Executive interview
rounds.notes: Product vision, strategic thinking and fit with Cisco's direction. Mostly for senior roles.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, ML experience and why Cisco. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Coding problems and multiple-choice questions, sometimes on networking fundamentals. Not used by every team. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML and statistics interview
rounds.notes: Statistics, modeling choices and evaluation, often framed around network telemetry, security or product data.

rounds.name: SQL and coding
rounds.notes: Live SQL and Python. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral
rounds.notes: STAR questions on ambiguous requirements, explaining results to non-technical people and teamwork.

rounds.name: Managerial final round
rounds.notes: Past projects end to end and long-term goals. Some candidates present a case study.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Networking background and certifications (CCNA, CCNP, CCIE). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Routing (OSPF, BGP), switching (VLANs, STP) and troubleshooting method through spoken scenarios.

rounds.name: Technical onsite rounds
rounds.notes: Several rounds on routing, switching, data center, security and network design; some whiteboard scenarios.

rounds.name: Hands-on lab
rounds.notes: Configure and troubleshoot devices or a simulation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral and customer focus
rounds.notes: Outages under pressure, customer interactions and teamwork.

question_patterns.pattern: A failure or mistake the candidate caused, how they owned it, who it affected, and what changed afterwards
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

question_patterns.pattern: A disagreement with a teammate or manager on a technical or product decision, how it was debated and how the candidate committed to the result
A time the candidate did more than required for a customer, or chose the customer's need over the easier engineering path
Delivering with a remote, cross-functional or very different team, and helping others succeed
An improvement to a process, tool or system the candidate started on their own, the risk involved and how it was managed
An outage, deadline or escalation handled under pressure, with the trade-offs made between speed and quality
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

question_patterns.pattern: Walk through the most complex project on the resume: own role, technical decisions, scale and measurable result
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

question_patterns.pattern: Why Cisco, which product area (networking, security, observability, collaboration) and how past skills fit the role
Explain a core protocol or OS concept (transport reliability, OSI layers, routing, concurrency) and when its trade-offs matter
Talk through a design for monitoring, configuring or controlling many network devices, including failure cases and rollback
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

question_patterns.pattern: Talk through a real-time or high-availability service such as video conferencing or a load balancer: latency, redundancy and graceful degradation
A systematic approach to diagnosing a connectivity, latency or production issue, layer by layer
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

question_patterns.theme: ML on network and security data
question_patterns.pattern: Modeling and evaluation choices for telemetry or security data: imbalance, anomaly detection, error trade-offs
Prioritize features or a roadmap for an enterprise networking, security or collaboration product with competing customers, sales and engineering needs
Improve a Cisco-style product for a specific enterprise user (IT admin, end user, buyer), with a success metric
Define how to measure success for a B2B product where buyers, admins and end users differ

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed. What did you do next?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real failure the candidate caused or could have prevented. Explain why the plan seemed right then, how the problem was found, and how quickly they owned it and told the people affected. Describe the fix and a concrete change in how they work, ideally with a later example where it paid off. Pitfalls: a disguised success, blaming others or circumstances, or a lesson with no visible change.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: Whether you own failures without blaming others
What you changed afterwards
strong_signals: Explains why the plan seemed right at the time
Owned it quickly and told those affected
Gives a later example of the lesson

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about how to do something. How was it resolved?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show the disagreement had real stakes. State the other person's view fairly, explain how the candidate raised the concern openly and used data, a prototype or a test to decide. Describe the outcome, including committing to a decision they did not prefer, and how the working relationship held up. Pitfalls: a story where the other person is simply wrong, going to the manager first, or avoiding the conflict.

looking_for: Whether you raise disagreement openly and respectfully
Whether you commit once a decision is made
strong_signals: States the other view fairly
Uses data or a test to decide
Shows the relationship afterwards
watch_outs: The other person is simply wrong
Escalating first or avoiding the conflict

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you went beyond what was asked to deliver for a customer or user.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the customer or user group and what was at stake for them (for example an outage, a missed deadline, a migration). Explain what the requirement was and what extra the candidate did and why. Quantify the result for the customer, such as downtime avoided or adoption. Show judgment about scope: doing more without derailing other commitments. Pitfalls: heroics without customer impact, or an internal stakeholder dressed up as a customer.

looking_for: How you think about customer outcomes
Whether you can show the result in numbers
strong_signals: Names the customer and what was at stake
Quantifies the customer result
Keeps other commitments on track

sample_questions.question: Describe a decision where what the customer needed and what was easiest for engineering pulled in different directions.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out both options and their costs: the convenient path and the customer-preferred one (for example backward compatibility, reliability, a harder migration). Explain how the candidate gathered evidence of customer impact, how they made the case to the team, and what was chosen. Strong answers favor reliability and the customer while staying realistic about cost, and show the result. Pitfalls: always choosing the easy path, or ignoring the engineering cost entirely.

looking_for: How you weigh customer needs against engineering cost
How you make the case to the team
strong_signals: Lays out both options and their costs
Uses evidence of customer impact
Favors reliability while staying realistic

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a process or tool you improved on your own initiative.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the pain the candidate noticed (slow builds, manual testing, noisy alerts), why no one owned it, and what they did without being asked. Explain how they limited the risk, got buy-in, and measured the result (time saved, fewer incidents). Small improvements are fine if the impact is clear. Pitfalls: an assigned task presented as initiative, or a change with no measured effect.

looking_for: Whether you improve things without being asked
How you manage the risk of a change
strong_signals: Names the pain and why no one owned it
Gets buy-in and limits risk
Measures the result
watch_outs: An assigned task presented as initiative

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you worked with a remote or distributed team to deliver something.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the context: teams in different time zones, functions or business units, and what had to be delivered together. Explain the concrete practices the candidate used (clear owners, written decisions, overlap hours, shared dashboards) and how they handled a misunderstanding or dependency slip. Show the result and how the other team saw the collaboration. Pitfalls: only describing meetings, or blaming the other location.

looking_for: How you collaborate across time zones and teams
How you handle dependency problems
strong_signals: Uses concrete practices like written decisions and clear owners
Handles a misunderstanding constructively
Shows the shared result

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to influence a team you had no authority over.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the team and the goal they did not share at first (for example engineering capacity or a sales priority). Explain how the candidate understood their incentives, built the case with customer data, found allies, and offered something in return. Show the result and what they would do differently. At senior levels the influence should span several teams. Pitfalls: escalating to a manager as the main tactic, or an outcome that was never really in doubt.

looking_for: How you influence without authority
Whether you understand other teams' incentives
strong_signals: Builds the case with customer data
Finds allies and offers something in return
Shows the result
watch_outs: An outcome that was never in doubt

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a network outage you handled under pressure.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the impact (users, sites, business) and the candidate's role. Walk through the triage: restoring service first, isolating the fault layer by layer, communicating status to the customer or stakeholders at a steady cadence. Then the root cause, the permanent fix and what was changed to prevent repeats (monitoring, change control). Pitfalls: guessing fixes without a method, silence toward stakeholders, or no follow-up after recovery.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: How you stay methodical under pressure
How you keep stakeholders informed
strong_signals: Restores service first, then finds root cause
Communicates status on a steady cadence
Adds prevention afterwards

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at Cisco, and which part of the business interests you?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a specific area (networking, security, observability, collaboration such as Webex, AI infrastructure) and connect it to the candidate's past work and goals. Show understanding of what Cisco builds and who its customers are, and how the candidate likes to work. Pitfalls: generic praise of the brand, talking only about stability or pay, or no named product area.

looking_for: Whether you know what Cisco builds
How your skills match the role
strong_signals: Names a specific product area
Links it to your past work
Shows who the customers are

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a complex data science project you led from scoping to deployment.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the business or customer problem and how it was turned into a modeling question. Cover data sources and quality issues, the baseline, model choice and evaluation metric, and why. Explain deployment, monitoring and how stakeholders used the result, with measured impact. Make the candidate's own decisions clear. Pitfalls: only describing algorithms, no baseline, or a model that never reached users.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: How you go from business problem to deployed model
Your own decisions in the project
strong_signals: Frames the business problem first
Compares against a baseline
Shows deployment, monitoring and impact
watch_outs: A model that never reached users

sample_questions.question: Which Cisco product would you most like to own, and what would success look like in your first 90 days?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick one product and show real understanding of its users, buyers and competition. For the first 90 days, describe listening first (customers, sales, engineering, support), learning the metrics and roadmap, then one or two early wins and a point of view on direction. Show how success would be judged. Pitfalls: proposing a big rewrite before learning, or a product chosen without knowing its customers.

looking_for: How well you know a Cisco product and its users
How you would start in a new role
strong_signals: Shows knowledge of users, buyers and competitors
Listens first, then picks early wins
Says how success is judged

sample_questions.question: Explain the difference between TCP and UDP, and when you would choose each.
sample_questions.strong_answer: TCP is connection-oriented: handshake, sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission for reliable in-order delivery, plus flow and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no delivery or order guarantee and little overhead. Choose TCP for data that must arrive intact (web, file transfer, APIs) and UDP where latency matters more than completeness (voice, video, DNS, telemetry), often with reliability added in the application or via protocols like QUIC. Pitfalls: saying UDP is simply faster without explaining why, or forgetting head-of-line blocking.

looking_for: How deeply you understand transport protocols
Whether you can pick one for a real use case
strong_signals: Explains handshake, acknowledgments and congestion control
Gives use cases for each
Mentions head-of-line blocking or QUIC

sample_questions.question: How would you design a monitoring system for thousands of network devices?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify device count, metrics, freshness and alerting needs. Compare polling (SNMP) with push-based streaming telemetry, and use collectors close to devices feeding a message queue and a time-series store with retention and downsampling. Cover threshold and anomaly alerts with deduplication, dashboards, and scaling collectors by partitioning devices. Discuss failure cases: a collector losing reach during a network partition, buffering, and avoiding alert storms. Pitfalls: one central poller, or no plan for the monitoring path itself failing.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: How you collect and store telemetry at scale
Whether you plan for network failures
strong_signals: Compares polling with push telemetry
Partitions devices across collectors
Handles partitions and alert storms
watch_outs: Ignoring failure of the monitoring path

sample_questions.question: How would you push a security policy to thousands of switches, and roll it back safely if it turns out to be wrong?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a central control plane with a versioned policy store and a declarative desired state. Validate policies before rollout, then deploy in stages (canary devices, one site, then wider) with health checks between waves. Devices report applied version and status; handle offline devices with reconciliation. For rollback, keep the previous version on device or in the store, apply atomically where possible, and stop the rollout automatically on errors, without dropping traffic. Pitfalls: pushing to all devices at once, or no record of which version each device runs.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: How you roll out changes to many devices safely
How you design for rollback
strong_signals: Uses versioned, declarative policy
Rolls out in waves with health checks
Tracks applied versions and reconciles offline devices
watch_outs: Pushing to all devices at once
No record of versions per device

sample_questions.question: How would you design a video conferencing service like Webex at large scale?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify meeting sizes, latency target and features (screen share, recording). Cover signaling separate from media, WebRTC-style media transport over UDP, media servers that forward streams (SFU) rather than mixing, regional placement close to users, and adaptive bitrate for poor networks. Discuss scaling large meetings, recording through a separate pipeline, encryption, and failover when a media server dies mid-meeting. Pitfalls: routing all media through one central region, or TCP-only media.

looking_for: How you handle real-time media at scale
Whether you plan for poor networks and failures
strong_signals: Separates signaling from media
Uses forwarding media servers near users
Adapts bitrate and handles server failover

sample_questions.question: How would you handle a heavily imbalanced dataset when building a security threat detection model?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the cost of errors: missed threats versus false alarms that tire analysts. Use metrics that fit imbalance (precision-recall curves, recall at a fixed false-positive rate) instead of accuracy. Options: resampling or class weights, anomaly detection for rare unseen attacks, better labels, and time-based splits to avoid leakage. Tune the threshold with the security team and monitor drift as attackers change. Pitfalls: reporting accuracy, random splits that leak future data, or ignoring analyst workload.

looking_for: How you evaluate models on rare events
Whether you weigh missed threats against false alarms
strong_signals: Uses precision-recall instead of accuracy
Splits by time to avoid leakage
Tunes the threshold with users and watches drift

sample_questions.question: A user reports they cannot reach an application. Walk me through how you would troubleshoot it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scope first: one user or many, one site or all, since when, what changed. Then work layer by layer: physical link and interface status, VLAN and switching, IP addressing and gateway, routing and reachability (ping, traceroute), DNS, firewall or ACL rules, and finally the application and server. Use logs and recent changes to narrow quickly, fix, confirm with the user and record the root cause. Pitfalls: random changes without a hypothesis, or skipping the question of what changed recently.
values: Execute with quality, urgency and accountability

looking_for: Whether you troubleshoot methodically
How you narrow the scope first
strong_signals: Asks about scope and recent changes first
Works layer by layer
Confirms the fix and records the cause

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize features for an enterprise networking product?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the product, its segment and the business goal (growth, retention, a competitive gap). Gather inputs from customers, sales, support and engineering, separating loud requests from broad needs. Score candidates on customer value, revenue or retention impact, strategic fit with the platform, and effort or risk, including hardware and backward-compatibility constraints. Recommend a short list, say what is cut and how it is communicated to sales and customers. Pitfalls: ranking by the largest customer's asks only, or ignoring engineering cost.

looking_for: How you prioritize across customers, sales and engineering
Whether you say what gets cut
strong_signals: Separates loud requests from broad needs
Scores by value, strategy and effort
Explains how cuts are communicated

sample_questions.question: How would you improve Webex for large enterprises?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the goal (adoption, retention, expansion) and separate the buyer (IT and procurement), admins and end users. Pick one segment, for example IT admins in very large deployments, and their pains (rollout, security policy, call quality visibility). Propose a few solutions, prioritize by impact and effort, recommend one, and define a success metric plus a guardrail such as meeting quality. Pitfalls: consumer-style feature ideas that ignore admins and buyers, or no metric.

looking_for: Whether you separate buyers, admins and end users
How you pick one problem and measure it
strong_signals: Picks one enterprise segment and its pains
Prioritizes by impact and effort
Defines a success metric and a guardrail

sample_questions.question: How would you measure success for a B2B networking product?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the product's purpose and its customers. Separate business outcomes (bookings, renewals, expansion), adoption (devices or sites deployed, features in use), customer health (support cases, uptime, time to deploy) and satisfaction. Pick one primary metric tied to the goal, add leading indicators and guardrails, and note B2B issues: long sales cycles, few large accounts, and partner channels that hide usage data. Pitfalls: consumer metrics like daily active users without adaptation, or revenue only.

looking_for: How you choose metrics for B2B products
Whether you account for long sales cycles
strong_signals: Separates business, adoption and health metrics
Picks one primary metric with leading indicators
Notes partner channels and few large accounts

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-defined tasks under guidance; strong CS and networking fundamentals; coding-focused loop, often with an online assessment.
Owns features independently within one team and may lead small projects; system design may be asked.
Leads design of a subsystem or product area, guides other engineers and works with adjacent teams; system design expected.
Sets technical direction across several teams or a product line and links engineering with senior management.
Shapes architecture and technology strategy for a business unit or across Cisco.
Owns features of an enterprise product with support; works with engineering, sales and support.
Owns a product area, its roadmap and metrics; aligns engineering, marketing, sales and channel partners.
Sets product strategy across a portfolio or platform and influences executive decisions.

persona.tone: Friendly, conversational and collaborative; wants to hear the candidate's own story
persona.pace: Moderate; works through resume and fundamentals before harder questions, with time to think
persona.pushback_style: Probes fundamentals ('why does that work at the protocol level?'), asks what the candidate personally did and for measurable results, and asks about failure cases and the customer impact
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions about the team and role

case_style.notes: PM cases are enterprise and B2B: roadmap prioritization, improving products such as Webex for admins and buyers, B2B metrics, and market or licensing strategy. Technical and platform constraints (scale, reliability, security, hardware) matter more than in consumer cases. Market sizing appears in some product cases.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the three Guiding Principles (Think Really Big, Play to Win, Drive Durable Growth, introduced FY2025) are official; we split them into seven principles using their published sub-points. Cisco does not say interviews score these principles, and prep sites still cite the older Conscious Culture (accountability, empathy, ethics).

loop_structure: Cisco's official page only says the process varies by team and role; round names, counts and durations come from prep sites and candidate reports. The hiring manager round duration and the network/customer experience engineer loop (role family other) are common-pattern estimates.
question_patterns: built from third-party prep sites and candidate reports, not from Cisco; topics vary widely between networking, security, Splunk observability and Webex teams.

bar_by_level: Cisco does not publish its ladder. Titles come from job postings and prep sites; numeric grades (reported roughly 4 to 12+ for engineers) are left out because sources disagree on the title-to-grade mapping. 'Senior Software Engineer' is mapped to mid because sources place it below Technical Leader. PM titles are our estimate.
persona: inferred from Cisco's recruiter tips ('tell us your story', measurable impact) and prep-site descriptions; no official description of interviewer style.

scoring_weights: our estimate from reported emphasis on fundamentals, accountability, collaboration and customer focus; prep sites claim behavioral topics carry about half the weight, which is unverified.
case_style: based on two PM prep guides; the split between product sense, estimation and system thinking is our estimate.
